rv.q: If neatness is what you expect from John Guare's 'A Free Man of Color,' you'll be doomed to disappointment. Mr. Guare's ambitious new play, which tells the fantastic tale of Jacques Cornet (Jeffrey Wright), a 19th-century millionaire playboy from New Orleans who happens to be black, has a cast of 33 and runs for 2½ crowded hours.
The self-conscious hodgepodge of styles and ideas can take a jerky, uneven rhythm, but there’s plenty here to dazzle the eye and occupy the mind.
That’s A Free Man of Color: It’s not a map, or even an atlas, but a huge, misshapen, distracted globe, one that even a theatrical Tamburlaine like Guare can’t quite figure out how to bestride.
Most of the show is a maddening slog. But the last 30 minutes are so brilliant that you can't dismiss the whole thing.
But the visual embellishments only add another layer of self-indulgence to a play already far too intoxicated with its own cleverness in juggling heady historical rumination with low comedy.
The sober racial history and the frivolous period stylization feel like incompatible systems, straining against each other while juggling too much information and not enough justification.
Within that multitude of names lies the essence and the central problem of "A Free Man of Color," which opened on Thursday in a Theater production.
Despite some dazzling writing, spectacular stage effects, a cast of thousands, and a lavish production budget, much of Guare’s ambitious work is reduced to a busy bore.
Even cut down to less than three, it still feels unwieldy.
If “A Free Man of Color” is not 24-karat gold, it glitters nonetheless.
But the result of a collision is usually painful and messy, and that's certainly the case at the Vivian Beaumont, despite the lavish and loving production.
Too bad it’s in a production that’s got more style than substance.
The play, which furiously flaps its wings under the hectic direction of George C. Wolfe, never gets off the ground.
This is one excruciating, headache-inducing evening of theater and a long one at that.
Complex, chaotic and teeming with detail, the sprawling play and its pell-mell production are sure to bewilder some viewers as much as they certainly will fascinate others.
Despite the production’s clever direction, gorgeous costumes, inventive sets, and skilled cast, it's a toughie.
The initial draft of John Guare’s new play "A Free Man of Color" apparently first arrived as a five-hour epic. Even cut down to less than three, it still feels unwieldy.

cn.t: Guare's wildly ambitious historical epic divides critics as a "glorious mess"—most find it overstuffed and unwieldy despite flashes of brilliance, though many praise its powerful final act.
